findings.title: canManage() grants manage permission when only VIEW scope is held
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70), the fallback permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it accepts the VIEW scope as sufficient for manage. Every other manage check in the same class (canManage(GroupModel) at line 79) correctly checks only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`. The consequence is that an admin granted only the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type (all groups) is treated as having full manage rights for realm-wide group operations such as creating top-level groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage()). This is a privilege-escalation bug: view-only admins can create, move, and delete groups. The check should be `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`.

findings.title: hasPermission looks up group resource by raw group id instead of schema resource name, and NPEs when the all-groups resource is missing
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String groupId, ...) resolves the per-group resource with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141). In the V2 schema (AdminPermissionsSchema), per-group resources are created with the group id as their name (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() and getOrCreateResource uses that as the resource name), so findByName works only if the resource was already created; however, when no per-group resource exists, the code falls back to the 'Groups' all-resource via `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` (line 144) and then immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 147) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (e.g. admin permissions were enabled but the schema resources were not initialized, or the feature was toggled), causing a NullPointerException instead of a clean 'false' denial. A null check (return false when resource == null) is required. Additionally, relying on findByName(groupId) means a group whose resource was never created silently falls back to the all-groups permission, which may grant unintended access if a broad all-groups permission exists while the intent was per-group scoping; the fallback should be explicit and safe.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds raw resource ids that are not group ids
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (lines 121-125), the code iterates resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. In the V2 schema, per-group resources are named with the group id but their resource id is an internal authorization-store id, not the group id. The returned set is consumed by UsersResource.searchForUser / BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser, which set it as the session attribute UserModel.GROUPS and pass it to user search/count queries that expect group ids (the V1 implementation in GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission strips the 'group.resource.' prefix from the resource name to recover the group id). Passing authorization resource ids as group ids means the user search filter matches nothing (or, worse, could match an unrelated group if ids collide), so admins with view-members permission on specific groups will not see the members they are entitled to see — a functional authorization bug. The group id should be recovered from the resource name (resource.getName()), consistent with the V1 implementation.

findings.title: hasPermission filters evaluated permissions by resource id, dropping permissions granted via the all-users resource
findings.body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) (lines 116-130), after evaluating `new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server)`, the code only accepts a permission if `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())` (line 123). When the per-user resource does not exist, `resource` is the 'Users' all-resource (line 109), and the evaluation engine returns permissions whose resourceId is the id of the resource the permission is actually attached to. Scope permissions created for the all-users resource evaluate against that resource, so this filter is consistent for the all-users case; however, when a per-user resource exists, permissions defined on the all-users resource (the documented fallback: 'check if there is permission for all-users') are evaluated by the engine but then discarded by this filter because their resourceId differs from the per-user resource id. This breaks the intended fallback semantics (a realm-wide 'view all users' permission no longer applies to a user that has its own resource), causing denial of access that admins configured. The filter should accept permissions matching either the per-user resource or the all-users resource type resource, or the evaluation should be performed per resource.

findings.title: Per-user resource lookup uses raw user id as resource name without existence guarantee, and all-users fallback can NPE
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission resolves the per-user resource with `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` (line 105). In the V2 schema, user resources are named with the user id (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveUser returns user.getId()), so this works only for resources already created by getOrCreateResource. When the per-user resource is absent, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 109) and then calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 111) without a null check; getResourceTypeResource returns null if the 'Users' resource does not exist, producing a NullPointerException instead of returning false. The same missing-null-check pattern exists in GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission. Both should return false (deny) when the fallback resource is null.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission matches resources by type 'Group' but V2 resources use type 'Groups', and name-prefix stripping is fragile
findings.body: GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (lines 313-317) iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)` and strips the 'group.resource.' prefix from resource names to recover group ids. This is the V1 evaluator, but MgmtPermissionsV2 now overrides groups() to return GroupPermissionsV2, so this V1 method is only used in V1 mode; however, the type string 'Group' (singular) versus the V2 schema's GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE ('Groups') shows the two evaluators use different resource type conventions, and any code path that mixes them (e.g. a realm migrated from V1 to V2 where resources were created with type 'Group') will silently return an empty set, breaking the group-based user visibility filter. The consequence is that admins lose visibility of users in groups they can view members of. The resource type lookup should be consistent (use AdminPermissionsSchema constants) or both types should be handled.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set when user can manage but not view, changing semantics from previous getGroupsWithViewPermission
findings.body: The old V1 method getGroupsWithViewPermission() returned an empty set when `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` (i.e. full access). The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 298) only checks `root.users().canView()`, omitting the canManage() case. An admin with manage-users but not view-users would previously get an empty set (meaning 'no group filter, see all users'), but now gets a set of group ids derived from view-members/manage-members permissions, which is likely empty — and an empty set is treated by callers (UsersResource.searchForUser: `if (!groupIds.isEmpty()) session.setAttribute(...)`) as 'no filter', so the outcome may be the same by accident, but the intermediate semantics differ and any future caller that distinguishes empty-set from null will misbehave. More importantly, in V1, canViewMembers(group) was true when `root.users().canView()`; the new canViewMembers also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE, which is a deliberate change, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's guard should mirror the old condition (canView() || canManage()) to preserve behavior for manage-only admins.

findings.title: canViewMembers now also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope, changing V1 semantics
findings.body: In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel) (line 340), the permission check was changed from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`. This means an admin granted only 'manage-members' on a group (without 'view-members') can now list group members via GroupResource.getMembers (which calls requireViewMembers). Whether this is intended is unclear — the V2 GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers does the same — but it is a behavioral change to the V1 evaluator that widens access: manage-members was previously not sufficient to view the member list. If the intent is that manage implies view, it should be documented; otherwise this is an unintended privilege widening in the legacy (non-V2) permission path.

findings.title: canList() reordered but semantics changed: QUERY_GROUPS alone no longer implies list when canView() is false in V2
findings.body: GroupPermissions.canList() was changed from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(VIEW_USERS, MANAGE_USERS, QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()`. Logically these are equivalent for the role check, but in V2, canView() is overridden by GroupPermissionsV2.canView() which additionally checks fine-grained permissions, so the behavior is preserved. However, the reordering means the fine-grained canView() is evaluated after the role check; this is fine. No concrete bug, but note that in V2, an admin with only a fine-grained 'view' permission on all groups (no admin roles) can now list groups — this is intended per the interface javadoc. Not reported as a defect; see other findings.

findings.title: canViewByGroup now uses canViewMembers which includes MANAGE_MEMBERS, widening V1 user visibility via group permissions
findings.body: In UserPermissions (V1), canViewByGroup(user) previously used `root.groups().getGroupsWithViewPermission(group)` which required VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE only. It now uses `root.groups()::canViewMembers`, and GroupPermissions.canViewMembers was simultaneously changed (line 340) to also accept MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE. The net effect in the V1 path: an admin with only 'manage-members' permission on a group (no view-members, no view-users role) can now see all users that are members of that group through the users search endpoint. This is a privilege widening in the legacy evaluator that was not part of the V2 feature; if manage-members is intended to imply viewing members, it should be an explicit, documented decision applied consistently, otherwise V1 behavior has silently changed for existing deployments.

findings.title: hasPermission(String...) lost the EvaluationContext overload visibility needed by subclasses
findings.body: UserPermissions.hasPermission(String... scopes) (line 486) delegates to a private hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...) (line 490). UserPermissionsV2 defines its own private hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) and does not reuse the parent's context-aware evaluation, which is fine, but the parent's `hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...)` being private means V2 cannot reuse the grantIfNoPermission fallback logic (line 501: `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`). In V2, UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission returns false when the resource server is null (line 101-103), whereas V1's grantIfNoPermission mechanism (set via usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(...) in UsersResource.toRepresentation when group-based filtering is active) allowed access when no permissions are configured. This means in V2, when an admin has group-based view permissions (UserModel.GROUPS session attribute set) but no user permissions configured, canView(user) may return false where V1 granted access, breaking the group-membership-based visibility flow. The V2 evaluator should honor the grantIfNoPermission flag similarly.

findings.title: Group-based user filtering now applied even when admin has full view-users permission, and grantIfNoPermission logic depends on session attribute
findings.body: In UsersResource.searchForUser (lines 448-451), the code now unconditionally sets the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute from `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` whenever the set is non-empty, removing the previous guard `if (!auth.users().canView())`. In V1, getGroupsWithViewPermission() returned an empty set when the admin had view/manage users, so the attribute was not set. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() also returns empty when root.users().canView(), so the guard removal is mostly harmless; however, toRepresentation (line 459) calls `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` — the grant decision now depends on whether the session attribute was set, which depends on whether getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returned a non-empty set. If an admin has view-members on some groups (non-empty set) but the user search should show all users (e.g. admin also has view-users via a role checked elsewhere), the attribute is set and grantIfNoPermission(true) is called, which in V1 grants manage+view when no user resource exists — potentially over-granting. The coupling between 'group filter active' and 'grant if no permission' is fragile and changed semantics; the condition should be based on `!auth.users().canView()` as before.

findings.title: Same unconditional group-filter change as UsersResource, with same grantIfNoPermission coupling
findings.body: BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser (lines 147-150) mirrors the UsersResource change: it now sets the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute whenever getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is non-empty, without checking `!auth.users().canView()` first, and toRepresentation (line 159) calls `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`. The consequence is identical to the UsersResource finding: the 'grant if no permission' fallback in the V1 evaluator is triggered by the presence of the session attribute rather than by the admin lacking view permission, which can grant view/manage on users to admins who actually have group-scoped permissions but no user permissions configured, and can suppress users that should be visible. The original guard `if (!auth.users().canView())` should be restored.

findings.title: getSubGroups filter change removes the canView-global bypass, but V2 canView(group) may not cover hierarchy semantics
findings.body: In GroupResource.getSubGroups (line 176-180), the filter was changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g)` (where canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView()) to simply `auth.groups()::canView`. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(group) returns true if canView() (global) OR canManage() OR per-group permission, so the behavior is equivalent. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group) returns true if the admin has MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles OR hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE). The subtle issue: in V2, an admin with a fine-grained 'view' permission on a parent group but not on child groups will not see the child groups in the children listing, whereas the previous code with canViewGlobal would show all children if the admin had global view. This is arguably correct for fine-grained permissions (per-group scoping), but it means the 'view' permission is no longer inherited down the group hierarchy — an admin with view on a parent group cannot see its subgroups unless they also have view on each subgroup or on all-groups. This is a significant semantic change for the subgroups listing endpoint that should be verified as intended; if hierarchy inheritance is expected, canView should walk up the parent chain like UserPermissions.evaluateHierarchy does for users.

findings.title: getGroups non-hierarchy path drops the global canView bypass, changing V1 behavior for admins with global view
findings.body: In GroupsResource.getGroups (line 113), the non-hierarchy path filter was changed from `g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g)` to `groupsEvaluator::canView`. In V1, GroupPermissions.canView(group) already includes the global canView()/canManage() check, so V1 behavior is preserved. In V2, GroupPermissionsV2.canView(group) checks admin roles (MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS) or per-group permission; an admin with a fine-grained 'view' permission on the all-groups resource (Groups resource type) but no per-group resource for a specific group will fail canView(group) because hasPermission(group.getId(), ...) finds no per-group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource only when the per-group resource is null — which it does (line 141-150 of GroupPermissionsV2), so the fallback works. However, the fallback only applies when the per-group resource does not exist; if a per-group resource exists (created by a previous permission) but has no policies granting this admin, hasPermission returns false without falling back to the all-groups resource. This means: once any permission is created for a specific group, admins with only all-groups view permission lose visibility of that group in the listing. This 'specific overrides global' behavior may be intended, but combined with the removal of the explicit global bypass it creates an inconsistency with the hierarchy path (populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups), which uses the evaluator differently. The behavior should be verified and ideally the fallback to the all-groups resource should also occur when the per-group resource exists but yields no permission.

findings.title: getScope NPEs when resourceType is not in the schema
findings.body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (line 238), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code calls `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` without checking that getResourceTypes().get(resourceType) is non-null. If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of Clients/Groups/Users (e.g. a legacy policy or a malformed request), this throws a NullPointerException instead of the intended ModelValidationException. The method should validate that the resource type exists and throw ModelValidationException('Resource type ... not found') similar to throwExceptionIfResourceTypeOrScopesNotProvided (line 220-222).

findings.title: getResourceName only handles Users resource type; Groups and Clients fall through to display name
findings.body: AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350) resolves a human-readable name only for the USERS resource type ('All users' or the username). For GROUPS and CLIENTS resource types, it returns resource.getDisplayName(), which for schema-created resources is typically null or the raw id, so admin UIs listing permissions for groups/clients will show unhelpful names. Since this PR adds the Groups resource type, getResourceName should be extended to resolve group names (and ideally client names) the same way resolveGroup/resolveClient do, otherwise the permission management UI will display broken labels for group permissions.

findings.title: registerListener now checks feature flag at registration time instead of event time, changing behavior for dynamically enabled features
findings.body: In AdminPermissions.registerListener (lines 73-99), the Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) check was moved from inside onEvent to the registration call itself. Previously, the listener was always registered and the feature check happened per event; now, if the feature is disabled at server startup (when registerListener is called), the listener is never registered, and enabling the feature later (e.g. via a restart-less config change or in tests that toggle the profile) will not register the cleanup listener. The consequence: when a group/role/client is removed, its permissions are not cleaned up (setPermissionsEnabled(false)), leaving orphaned authorization resources. The check should remain inside onEvent, or the listener should be registered unconditionally as before.

findings.title: canMapRole now requires MANAGE_USERS role directly, removing V1 fine-grained users manage fallback
findings.body: In RolePermissions.canMapRole (line 302), the check was changed from `root.users().canManageDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)`. canManageDefault() was exactly `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` in UserPermissions (removed in this PR), so for V1 the behavior is identical. However, in V2, UserPermissionsV2.canManage() additionally grants manage when the admin has a fine-grained 'manage' permission on users (all-users or per-user). By bypassing root.users().canManage() and checking only the role, V2 admins who were granted fine-grained manage-users permission (but not the manage-users role) can no longer map roles, even though they can manage users. This is an inconsistency introduced by the refactor: role mapping should use root.users().canManage() (the evaluator), not the raw role check, so that V2 fine-grained permissions are honored.

findings.title: V1 canManage()/canView() changed from users-based defaults to direct role checks, dropping fine-grained user permission fallback
findings.body: In GroupPermissions (V1 class, but also the base for V2), canManage() was changed from `root.users().canManageDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` (line 274-276), and canView() from `root.users().canViewDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (line 286-288). In V1, canManageDefault/canViewDefault were exactly these role checks, so V1 behavior is unchanged. But GroupPermissionsV2 overrides canManage()/canView() with fine-grained checks, so V2 is fine. The issue: any other V1 code path that relied on GroupPermissions.canManage() honoring fine-grained user permissions (via root.users().canManage()) now does not. Since UserPermissions.canManage() in V1 also checks hasPermission(MANAGE_SCOPE) (fine-grained), the old canManageDefault() bypassed that too, so this is consistent with V1. However, the removal of canManageDefault/canViewDefault from UserPermissions (lines removed in the diff) means RolePermissions.canMapRole (which used canManageDefault) had to be changed to a raw role check, losing V2 fine-grained support (see separate finding). The net effect is that V2 fine-grained 'manage users' permission no longer implies group manage capabilities through the users evaluator, which may be intended but breaks the documented interface contract in GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() ('Or if it has a permission to MANAGE the group') — actually it checks group permission, so it's consistent. The real regression is in RolePermissions.canMapRole as reported separately.

findings.title: canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope in addition to their specific scope, widening V2 permissions
findings.body: In UserPermissionsV2, canMapRoles(user) (line 82) was changed from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)`, and canManageGroupMembership(user) (line 91) similarly now accepts MANAGE. Previously (in the base diff), canMapRoles checked `canManage(user)` first (which includes MANAGE), so accepting MANAGE is consistent with the old behavior; the change actually restores the 'manage implies map-roles' semantics that the intermediate version had removed. However, the interface javadoc for UserPermissionEvaluator.canMapRoles says 'MANAGE the user or MAP_ROLES of the user', so this is consistent. The concern: canManageByGroup(user) is now also OR-ed in, meaning an admin with manage-members on a group containing the user can map roles for that user. The interface javadoc explicitly documents this ('Or if it has a permission to MANAGE_MEMBERS of the group chain'), so it is intended. Not a defect per se, but the combination means 'manage-members' on a group grants role-mapping rights on all users in that group, which is a significant capability; this should be verified as intended by the security team.

findings.title: V2 canView/canManage removed AdminRoles.ADMIN from the role check
findings.body: In UserPermissionsV2.canView(user) and canManage(user) (lines 47-62), the role check was changed from `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (removing AdminRoles.ADMIN). AdminRoles.ADMIN is the 'admin' role in the master realm; hasOneAdminRole typically already accounts for realm-admin composite roles, but if an admin has only the 'admin' role (master realm admin managing another realm), the isAdminSameRealm() check would return false anyway, so the removal may be intentional. However, if hasOneAdminRole(ADMIN) was previously needed for same-realm admins with the 'admin' role (unusual but possible in custom setups), removing it could lock out such admins in V2. This should be verified against hasOneAdminRole semantics; if hasOneAdminRole already expands composites, the change is safe.

findings.title: Double semicolon in field declaration
findings.body: Line 68: `private final GroupRepresentation topGroup = new GroupRepresentation();;` contains a stray double semicolon. Harmless but should be cleaned up.

findings.title: testManageAllGroups creates a group with a blank name and expects FORBIDDEN, but the assertion may pass for the wrong reason
findings.body: In testManageAllGroups (line 141), the test calls `groups().add(new GroupRepresentation())` (blank name) and expects 403 FORBIDDEN. The server-side GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup checks `auth.groups().requireManage()` before validating the group name (line 181-189), so the 403 is due to missing permission, which is the intent. However, if the permission check were accidentally reordered after name validation, the test would get 400 and fail — so the test does guard the order. But the test does not verify that after granting MANAGE, creating a group with a blank name returns 400 (validation still works). More importantly, the test at line 146 adds a child with a blank name and expects 403; same reasoning. These are acceptable, but the test would be more robust using a named group to avoid conflating validation errors with permission errors. Not a blocking issue.

findings.title: testManageAllGroups expects NO_CONTENT for subGroup with an existing group id, but the server returns 204 only when moving an existing group; the test may be asserting move semantics unintentionally
findings.body: In testManageAllGroups (line 174), after creating 'testGroup' (which gets id testGroupId), the test calls `groups().group(topGroup.getId()).subGroup(group)` where group has an id set. GroupResource.addChild with a non-null rep.getId() moves the existing group under topGroup and returns 204 (builder initialized to 204, only set to 201 in the create branch). The test asserts NO_CONTENT (204), which matches the move path. This is intentional per the comment 'it should be possible to add the child to the group now', but the test name and flow suggest testing child creation; using an existing group id tests the move path, not creation. The permission check exercised is requireManage(group) on the parent, which is the same for both paths, so the test is valid for permission coverage but misleadingly named. Consider adding a separate assertion for creating a new child with a fresh name (no id) to cover the create path under the all-groups manage permission.

findings.title: testManageGroupMembership does not verify the negative case after granting permissions (no assertion that joinGroup with invalid group fails with NotFound rather than Forbidden)
findings.body: In testManageGroupMembership (line 306), after granting MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP on all-users and MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP on topGroup, the test calls `users().get(bobId).joinGroup(topGroup.getId())` and expects success (no exception). It does not verify that joining a non-existent group now returns NotFoundException (proving the permission check passed and the failure moved to group lookup), nor does it verify that myadmin still cannot manage membership of a group without MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP. The test would pass even if the permission check were silently bypassed (e.g. if the evaluator always returned true), because no negative control is present after the grant. Add an assertion that joining a different group without permission still throws ForbiddenException.

findings.title: Adding QUERY_GROUPS role to myadmin may mask fine-grained permission denials in group listing tests
findings.body: RealmAdminPermissionsConfig now grants myadmin the QUERY_GROUPS role (line 34-36). In V2, GroupPermissionsV2 inherits canList() from GroupPermissions, which returns `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()`. With QUERY_GROUPS, canList() is always true, so the groups listing endpoint is accessible regardless of fine-grained permissions. The testViewGroups test (GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest line 250) expects myadmin to see 0 groups initially and 1 group after granting VIEW on a specific group; this works because the listing filters by canView(group), not canList. However, the QUERY_GROUPS role means the test does not verify that an admin without any group-related role or permission gets 403 on the groups endpoint. The UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest previously relied on myadmin having only QUERY_USERS; adding QUERY_GROUPS changes the baseline for all tests in this config. If the intent is to test fine-grained group permissions in isolation, QUERY_GROUPS should not be granted, or a separate admin user without it should be used for the group tests.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission evaluates permissions per group resource in a loop, causing N permission evaluations per request
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 106-128) iterates all group resources via resourceStore.findByType and calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) for each, which triggers a full policy evaluation (root.evaluatePermission) per group. For realms with many groups, this is O(N) policy evaluations on every user search/count request that goes through UsersResource.searchForUser or getUsersCount (when the admin lacks global view-users). The V1 implementation (GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) has the same pattern, so this is not a regression, but the V2 implementation could batch-evaluate permissions for all resources in one call (the evaluation engine supports evaluating multiple ResourcePermissions). Given that this runs on the hot path of user listing, the performance impact for large realms should be assessed; at minimum, the per-resource evaluation should be short-circuited or cached per request.

findings.title: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods, but GroupResource still exposes management/permissions endpoints
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, getPermissions, etc. (lines 167-210). However, GroupResource.getManagementPermissions (line 321-330) and setManagementPermissionsEnabled (line 354-365) call `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` which returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when the V2 feature is enabled, and then call permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group) / setPermissionsEnabled / resource / getPermissions. In V2 mode, these calls will throw UnsupportedOperationException, resulting in a 500 error for the group management/permissions endpoints. The endpoints are guarded by `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` (V1 feature), not the V2 feature, so in a V2-enabled realm with V1 feature also enabled (or during transition), the endpoints are reachable and will crash. Either the endpoints should be disabled/guarded when V2 is active, or GroupPermissionsV2 should implement these methods (e.g. isPermissionsEnabled could check if any permission exists for the group resource). As written, this is a runtime 500 for any admin UI or client that queries group management permissions in a V2 realm.

findings.title: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods still used by UserResource management endpoints
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, managePermission, viewPermission, etc. (lines 152-199). UserResource exposes management/permissions endpoints (getManagementPermissions, setManagementPermissionsEnabled) that call AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).users().isPermissionsEnabled() / setPermissionsEnabled / getPermissions. In a V2-enabled realm, these calls throw UnsupportedOperationException, causing 500 errors. The endpoints are not guarded by a V2 feature check (they use ProfileHelper.requireFeature(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) which is the V1 feature). This is a runtime break for the user management permissions API in V2 mode. The endpoints should be guarded to return 404/400 when V2 is active, or the V2 evaluator should implement the management interface.

findings.title: isImpersonatable throws UnsupportedOperationException but is still called by V1 code paths (canClientImpersonate in UserPermissions)
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable(UserModel, ClientModel) and isImpersonatable(UserModel) throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 142-149). However, the base class UserPermissions.canClientImpersonate (line 340-353) calls `canImpersonate(context) && isImpersonatable(user)`, and UserPermissionsV2 overrides canClientImpersonate to delegate to canImpersonate(user, client) (line 137-139), so canClientImpersonate is safe. But any other caller of isImpersonatable (e.g. legacy code or the deprecated interface method) will crash in V2. The interface UserPermissionEvaluator still declares isImpersonatable as @Deprecated but not removed; if it is part of the public-ish contract used by extensions, throwing UnsupportedOperationException is a break. The method should either be implemented in V2 (e.g. return true, as V1 does when no user-impersonated permission is configured) or the interface should be cleaned up to remove the deprecated method and update all callers.

findings.title: canView() and canManage() use hasPermission(null, ...) which falls back to all-groups resource, but the policyStore.findByResource check may return empty for resource-type permissions
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canView() (line 52) and canManage() (line 70), hasPermission(null, scopes) is called with groupId=null. In hasPermission (line 141), when groupId is null, resource is null, so the code goes to the fallback: it loads the all-groups resource via getResourceTypeResource and checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` (line 147). This checks for policies directly associated with the all-groups resource. However, scope permissions in Keycloak are policies of type 'scope' that reference resources; findByResource should return them. If the permission was created with resourceType='Groups' (as the tests do via createAllPermission), the policy is associated with the 'Groups' resource, so findByResource returns non-empty. This seems correct. But note: if the admin has a permission on a specific group resource (not all-groups), canView() (global) returns false, which is correct. No concrete bug, but the interplay between per-group and all-groups fallback in hasPermission (lines 141-150) means that when a per-group resource exists but has no granting permission, the all-groups fallback is NOT consulted (the code returns the per-group resource and evaluates it, and if no permission matches, returns false at line 164). This means a specific group resource's existence 'shadows' the all-groups permission: an admin with view on all-groups loses view on any group that has its own resource (even if that resource has no policies granting the admin). This is the same shadowing issue noted for UsersResource; it should be verified as intended or fixed by also evaluating the all-groups resource when the per-group evaluation yields no permission.

findings.title: getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException for unknown resource type, but callers may expect null return
findings.body: In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 107-112), the switch on resourceType throws IllegalStateException for unknown types. Previously, the code returned null name for unknown types and then threw IllegalStateException at line 114-116 ('Could not map resource object...'). The behavior is similar (exception), but the exception type/message changed. Callers that catch IllegalStateException with the old message or that expected a null return for unsupported types (e.g. when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false, the method returns null at line 93-95) may now get an unexpected exception for a resource type that is simply not yet supported (e.g. 'Roles' if added later). This is a minor API contract change; the method should either return null for unknown types (consistent with the supportsAuthorizationSchema=false path) or the javadoc should document the exception.

findings.title: groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2 but the field type and superclass method signature use GroupPermissions, hiding V2-specific UnsupportedOperationException methods
findings.body: MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() (line 58-62) returns GroupPermissions (the superclass type), instantiated as GroupPermissionsV2. Callers that need V2-specific behavior must cast. More importantly, the AdminPermissionEvaluator interface (and AdminPermissionManagement) declare groups() returning GroupPermissionEvaluator / GroupPermissionManagement; the V2 implementation throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods. This is a design smell: the V2 evaluator implements the full management interface but throws for most methods, which is error-prone. A separate V2 management interface (or null-returning defaults) would be cleaner. Not a functional bug per se, but it means any code path that calls management methods on the evaluator (rather than on a management-specific instance) will crash in V2. The GroupResource/UserResource management endpoints are the concrete victims (see separate findings).

findings.title: getUsersCount with search='id:...' checks canView(userModel) but does not account for group-based visibility
findings.body: In UsersResource.getUsersCount (line 392-394), when search starts with 'id:', the code returns `userModel != null && userPermissionEvaluator.canView(userModel) ? 1 : 0`. In V2, UserPermissionsV2.canView(user) includes canViewByGroup(user), so group-based visibility is honored. In V1, UserPermissions.canView(user) also includes canViewByGroup. So this is consistent. However, the count endpoint does not set the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute (unlike searchForUser), so canViewByGroup relies on root.groups().canViewMembers(group) which evaluates permissions per group — this works without the session attribute. No bug. But note: the count endpoint for the non-id search path (lines 395-431) uses `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` to filter counts, which in V2 returns resource ids (see separate finding about getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adding resource ids instead of group ids). This means getUsersCount with group-scoped admin will return 0 (or wrong counts) because the group id filter uses authorization resource ids. This is the same root cause as the getGroupIdsWithViewPermission finding but manifests in the count endpoint.

findings.title: canManageMembership accepts MANAGE scope on the group, but manage-membership is a distinct, narrower capability
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership(group) (line 102), the permission check is `hasPermission(group.getId(), AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP)`. This means an admin with the 'manage' scope on a group (full group management) can also manage membership (add/remove users). This is consistent with the interface javadoc ('MANAGE the group or MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP of the group'). However, the V1 GroupPermissions.canManageMembership (line 358-366) checks `canManage(group)` first (which includes global manage) and then MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP_SCOPE only — it does NOT accept the group's MANAGE scope as sufficient for membership management when the admin lacks the global role. Wait, V1 canManage(group) returns true if canManage() (global role) OR per-group MANAGE_SCOPE; so in V1, having per-group 'manage' scope also grants manage-membership. So V2 is consistent with V1. The semantic question: should 'manage' on a group imply 'manage-membership'? The interface javadoc says yes. Not a defect, but worth noting that 'manage' is a powerful scope that includes membership management, which may surprise admins who expect manage to only cover group attributes.

findings.title: Interface javadoc for canManage() says 'For V2 only: Also if it has permission to VIEW or MANAGE groups' — should say MANAGE only
findings.body: In GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() javadoc (lines 72-78), it states 'For V2 only: Also if it has permission to AdminPermissionsSchema#VIEW or AdminPermissionsSchema#MANAGE groups.' However, GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) checks `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` — which, due to the bug reported separately, accepts VIEW as sufficient for manage. The javadoc says VIEW or MANAGE, matching the (buggy) implementation. If the implementation is fixed to check only MANAGE (as canManage(group) does), the javadoc must be updated to say 'MANAGE groups' only. The javadoc currently documents the buggy behavior, which is a documentation defect that would mislead maintainers fixing the bug.

findings.title: requireManageMembers javadoc incorrectly references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers
findings.body: In GroupPermissionEvaluator (line 132-135), the javadoc for requireManageMembers says 'Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} returns {@code false}.' It should reference #canManageMembers(GroupModel). This is a copy-paste error in the documentation that misleads readers about which permission is enforced.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc says 'If UserPermissionEvaluator#canView() evaluates to true, returns empty set' but implementation also checks canManage in V1
findings.body: The javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 142-147) states: 'If UserPermissionEvaluator#canView() evaluates to true, returns empty set.' However, the V1 implementation (GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, line 298) checks `root.users().canView()` only (the canManage check was removed in this PR; previously getGroupsWithViewPermission checked canView() || canManage()). The V2 implementation (GroupPermissionsV2 line 107) also checks only canView(). The javadoc is accurate for the new implementation but the semantics changed from the old method (which returned empty for canView || canManage). The javadoc should also mention that an empty set means 'no group-based filtering' and that callers interpret it as 'see all users', to make the contract clear.

findings.title: grantIfNoPermission fallback grants both MANAGE and VIEW only when both scopes are expected; V2 does not honor this flag
findings.body: In UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 500-502), when the Users resource does not exist (permissions not initialized), the method returns `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`. This is a legacy fallback: when fine-grained permissions are not configured for users, and the caller has set grantIfNoPermission=true (which UsersResource.toRepresentation does when group-based filtering is active), the admin is granted access. The condition requires BOTH manage and view scopes to be in the expected scopes, which is unusual (most callers check one or the other). This means the fallback rarely triggers as intended. In V2, UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission does not implement this fallback at all (returns false when resource server is null or resource is null and no all-users permission exists). The consequence: in V2, when an admin has group-based view permissions (session attribute set) but no user permissions configured, canView(user) returns false for users not in the admin's groups, which is correct, but for users in the admin's groups, canViewByGroup(user) should return true — this works. The grantIfNoPermission flag is a V1 mechanism to handle the case where permissions are not initialized; its absence in V2 means V2 relies on the all-users resource existing (created by AdminPermissionsSchema.init). If init was not called (e.g. admin permissions enabled but schema not initialized), V2 denies everything, which is safe but may break flows that worked in V1. This should be verified as intended.

findings.title: canViewMembers and canManageMembers do not check isAdminSameRealm before evaluating permissions
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers(group) (line 83-87) and canManageMembers(group) (line 89-94), the methods check `root.users().canView()` / `root.users().canManage()` first, then call hasPermission(group.getId(), ...). The private hasPermission method (line 130-133) does check `root.isAdminSameRealm()` and returns false if not same realm. So cross-realm admins are correctly denied. However, the V1 GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341) explicitly checks `root.isAdminSameRealm()` before evaluating, and returns false early. The V2 methods rely on hasPermission's internal check, which is fine. But note: canViewMembers first checks `root.users().canView()` — in V2, UserPermissionsV2.canView() checks admin roles and fine-grained permissions but does NOT check isAdminSameRealm() (the base UserPermissions.canView does check isAdminSameRealm at line 302-304, but UserPermissionsV2.canView() overrides it and does not call super, so the isAdminSameRealm check is skipped!). Wait, UserPermissionsV2.canView() (line 47-53) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS, VIEW_USERS)` — hasOneAdminRole presumably checks the admin's roles in the admins realm; for cross-realm admins, this could return true if the admin has manage-users in their own realm but is managing a different realm. The base UserPermissions.canView() explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. UserPermissionsV2.canView() omits this check, meaning a cross-realm admin with manage-users role in the master realm could get canView()=true in a managed realm, and then GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers would return true for any group, leaking member lists cross-realm. This is a potential cross-realm authorization bypass in V2. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added to UserPermissionsV2.canView()/canManage() or to hasPermission (which does check it, but canView() returns true before reaching hasPermission when the role check passes).

findings.title: V2 canView()/canManage() omit the isAdminSameRealm check, enabling cross-realm access for admins with realm-management roles
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.canView(user) (line 47-53) and canManage(user) (line 55-62) check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` and return true immediately, without verifying `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V1 base class UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()` before evaluating permissions. In Keycloak, an admin from the master realm (or another realm) with the manage-users/view-users role in their own realm should NOT automatically have those rights in a different realm they are managing (unless they are realm-admin of that realm). hasOneAdminRole checks the admin's roles, which for a master-realm admin include master realm roles; if the admin has 'manage-users' in master, hasOneAdminRole returns true, and V2 canView() returns true even when managing a different realm. This bypasses the cross-realm protection that V1 enforces. The consequence: a master-realm admin with manage-users (a common setup for realm management) gains view/manage access to all users in every realm they can access, even without being admin of those realms. The isAdminSameRealm() check (or an equivalent adminsRealm == realm check) must be added to UserPermissionsV2.canView(), canManage(), canMapRoles(), canManageGroupMembership(), and canImpersonate() before the role check returns true.

findings.title: V2 group canView()/canManage() omit isAdminSameRealm check, enabling cross-realm group access
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.canView() (line 47-53), canView(group) (line 55-62), canManage() (line 64-71), and canManage(group) (line 73-80) all check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (or MANAGE_USERS) and return true without verifying `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V1 GroupPermissions.canView(group) (line 254-264) explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. As with the UserPermissionsV2 finding, a master-realm admin with manage-users/view-users roles would get canView()/canManage() = true in any realm they manage, bypassing the cross-realm restriction. This grants cross-realm group visibility and management. The isAdminSameRealm() check must be added before the role-based early return in all four methods (or in hasPermission, but the role check returns before hasPermission is reached).

findings.title: canImpersonate does not check isAdminSameRealm before evaluating fine-grained permission
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.canImpersonate(user, requester) (line 65-74) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(ImpersonationConstants.IMPERSONATION_ROLE)` and returns true, then evaluates hasPermission(user, context, IMPERSONATE). The private hasPermission (line 94-97) does check `root.isAdminSameRealm()` and returns false if not same realm. However, the role check at line 66 returns true before hasPermission is called, so a cross-realm admin with the impersonation role gets impersonation rights in any realm. The V1 UserPermissions.canImpersonate() (line 411-421) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(ImpersonationConstants.IMPERSONATION_ROLE)` and then `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before evaluating. The V2 override omits the isAdminSameRealm check entirely. This is a cross-realm impersonation bypass: an admin with the impersonation role in their home realm can impersonate users in any realm they can access. The isAdminSameRealm() check must be added.

findings.title: canManageMembership checks MANAGE_USERS role without isAdminSameRealm guard
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership(group) (line 96-103) checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` and returns true without an isAdminSameRealm check. The V1 GroupPermissions.canManageMembership (line 358-366) checks `canManage(group)` first (which includes the isAdminSameRealm check via canManage(group) -> canManage() -> role check + isAdminSameRealm in hasPermission path... actually V1 canManage(group) checks canManage() which is role-only, then isAdminSameRealm, then hasPermission). In V1, canManage() is role-only (no isAdminSameRealm), but canManage(group) checks `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before hasPermission. So V1 denies cross-realm. V2 canManageMembership returns true for cross-realm admins with manage-users role. This allows a master-realm admin to manage group membership in any realm. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added.

findings.title: canViewMembers/canManageMembers rely on root.users().canView()/canManage() which in V2 lack isAdminSameRealm check
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers(group) (line 83-87) returns true if `root.users().canView()` is true. In V2, root.users() is UserPermissionsV2, whose canView() (as reported separately) lacks the isAdminSameRealm check. Therefore, a cross-realm admin with view-users role gets canViewMembers=true for all groups in the managed realm, leaking member lists. Similarly canManageMembers (line 89-94) uses root.users().canManage(). The V1 GroupPermissions.canViewMembers (line 330-341) checks `root.users().canView()` (V1 UserPermissions.canView which HAS the isAdminSameRealm check) and then explicitly checks isAdminSameRealm. The V2 chain loses both guards. This is a cross-realm member-list disclosure. Fixing UserPermissionsV2.canView()/canManage() to include isAdminSameRealm (as reported) resolves this, but an explicit guard here is also advisable.

findings.title: canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership check MANAGE_USERS role without isAdminSameRealm guard
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles(user) (line 77-83) and canManageGroupMembership(user) (line 85-92) check `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` and return true without an isAdminSameRealm check. The V1 UserPermissions.canMapRoles (line 442-451) checks `canManage(user)` first (which includes isAdminSameRealm via canManage -> hasPermission path... actually V1 canManage(user) = canManage() || canManageByGroup(user); canManage() checks isAdminSameRealm at line 238-240). So V1 denies cross-realm. V2 allows cross-realm admins with manage-users role to map roles and manage group membership in any realm. The isAdminSameRealm check must be added.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE and MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE but resource names use 'group.resource.' prefix; if V2 resources coexist, type mismatch causes empty results
findings.body: The V1 GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313) iterates resources of type 'Group' (singular) and strips the 'group.resource.' prefix. In a realm where V2 was enabled and group resources were created with type 'Groups' (GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and names equal to group ids (no prefix), this V1 method (if ever invoked in a mixed state) would find no resources of type 'Group' and return an empty set. An empty set is interpreted by callers as 'no group filter' (see UsersResource.searchForUser: `if (!groupIds.isEmpty())`), meaning the admin would see ALL users instead of only group members — a data exposure bug in mixed V1/V2 states. However, since MgmtPermissionsV2 overrides groups() to return GroupPermissionsV2, the V1 method is not used in V2 mode. The risk is during migration or if any code path constructs GroupPermissions directly. The type constant should be unified.

findings.title: Resource lookup by group id as name assumes resources are named with group ids; if a group is renamed or resource naming changes, permissions silently fail
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission resolves per-group resources with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141). The V2 schema (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup) creates resources named with the group id, so this works. However, group ids are immutable in Keycloak, so this is stable. But if a group is deleted and a new group is created with the same id (not possible in Keycloak — ids are UUIDs), or if the resource was created with a different naming convention (e.g. by an older V2 version or manual creation), the lookup fails and the code falls back to the all-groups resource. If the all-groups resource has permissions for the admin, access is granted based on the all-groups permission even though the intent was per-group — this is the shadowing issue. The fallback should be explicit: if the per-group resource does not exist, the permission should be evaluated against the all-groups resource ONLY (which is what happens), but if the per-group resource exists and yields no permission, the all-groups resource should ALSO be evaluated as a fallback (currently it is not). This means: create a per-group resource (e.g. by creating any permission for that group), and all admins with all-groups view permission lose access to that group. This is a data/authorization consistency issue.

findings.title: Same shadowing issue as groups: per-user resource existence blocks all-users fallback
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105-114) resolves the per-user resource by name (user id). If it exists, the all-users resource is never consulted, even if the per-user resource has no policies granting the admin. This means: once a permission is created for a specific user (creating the user resource), admins with all-users view permission lose access to that user. The V1 UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 497-521) always evaluates the single 'Users' resource (there are no per-user resources in V1), so this shadowing is a V2-specific behavior. The intended semantics (per the comment at line 108: 'check if there is permission for all-users. If so, load its resource and proceed with evaluation') suggest the all-users resource should be a fallback when the per-user resource yields no permission, not only when the per-user resource is absent. The current code only falls back when the per-user resource is null. This should be fixed by evaluating both resources and OR-ing the results, or by documenting that per-user resources override all-users permissions entirely.

findings.title: Resource name for groups is the group id, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() — if a group is looked up by a different identifier (e.g. path), the resource name may not match
findings.body: AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup (line 181-186) returns group.getId() as the resource name. GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission looks up resources by group.getId() as the name. This is consistent. However, if any code path creates a group resource with a different name (e.g. using the group path or name), the lookup fails. The schema's getOrCreateResource is the canonical creation path, so this should be consistent. Not a concrete bug, but the coupling between resource naming and group id should be documented.

findings.title: Scope name constants duplicated between GroupPermissions and AdminPermissionsSchema
findings.body: GroupPermissions defines MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP_SCOPE = 'manage-membership', MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE = 'manage-members', VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE = 'view-members' (lines 50-52), which are identical to AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP, MANAGE_MEMBERS, VIEW_MEMBERS. The duplication risks drift if scope names change. The class should reference AdminPermissionsSchema constants instead of redefining them. This is a maintainability issue, not a functional bug.

findings.title: Scope name constants duplicated between UserPermissions and AdminPermissionsSchema
findings.body: UserPermissions defines MAP_ROLES_SCOPE='map-roles', IMPERSONATE_SCOPE='impersonate', MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP_SCOPE='manage-group-membership' (lines 62-65), duplicating AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES, IMPERSONATE, MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP. Same maintainability concern as the GroupPermissions finding.

findings.title: hasPermission method name overloaded with different semantics from parent class
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2 defines a private hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes) (line 130) that has completely different semantics from the parent GroupPermissions.hasPermission(GroupModel, String...) and hasPermission(Resource, EvaluationContext, String...). The parent methods are still inherited and used by V1 code paths (e.g. canView(group) in the parent is overridden, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission in the parent uses the parent's hasPermission). The overloading with different parameter types (String vs GroupModel/Resource) is confusing and error-prone. The V2 method should be renamed (e.g. hasGroupPermission or evaluateGroupPermission) to avoid confusion.

findings.title: hasPermission method name overloaded with different semantics from parent class
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2 defines a private hasPermission(UserModel, EvaluationContext, String...) (line 94) that differs from the parent's protected hasPermission(String...) and private hasPermission(EvaluationContext, String...). The V2 method takes a UserModel as the first parameter, making it distinct, but the naming overlap is confusing. Rename to evaluateUserPermission for clarity.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission in V2 does not exclude the all-groups resource itself from the granted set
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 121-125) iterates all resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` for those where the admin has VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS. The all-groups resource (named 'Groups', type 'Groups') is also of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE. If the admin has a permission on the all-groups resource granting VIEW_MEMBERS, the all-groups resource's id is added to the granted set. This id is not a group id, so when passed to user search as a group filter, it matches nothing (or potentially a group with that id, which is unlikely). The result: the admin's group-based user visibility is broken (they see no users via group filter) even though they have view-members on all groups. The all-groups resource should be excluded from the iteration, or the method should return an empty set (meaning 'no filter, see all') when the all-groups resource grants view-members. The V1 implementation (GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) iterates type 'Group' (singular), which excludes the all-groups resource (which has no type or a different type in V1), so this is a V2-specific bug.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds resource ids, not group ids, and includes the all-groups resource id
findings.body: As noted in the earlier finding, GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource id) to the granted set, but callers (UsersResource.searchForUser, getUsersCount, BruteForceUsersResource) use this set as group ids for filtering users by group membership. The resource id is not the group id. In the V2 schema, per-group resources are named with the group id, so the correct value to add is `groupResource.getName()` (which is the group id), not `groupResource.getId()`. Additionally, the all-groups resource (named 'Groups') is of the same type and would be included if the admin has view-members on it; its name is 'Groups', not a group id, so it must be excluded. The consequence: user search and count with group-scoped admins returns wrong results (no users or wrong counts) because the filter uses non-existent group ids. This is a functional break of the group-membership-based user visibility feature in V2.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission strips 'group.resource.' prefix from resource name, but if a resource name does not have the prefix (e.g. all-groups resource), substring produces garbage
findings.body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313-317), the code iterates resources of type 'Group' and does `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())` to recover the group id. If a resource of type 'Group' has a name shorter than the prefix or without the prefix (e.g. manually created, or the all-groups resource if it were typed 'Group'), the substring produces a garbage string or throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The all-groups resource in V1 is named 'Users' for users (UserPermissions.USERS_RESOURCE) but for groups, the V1 initialize method creates resources named 'group.resource.<id>' with type 'Group' (line 117), so all type-'Group' resources have the prefix. However, the V2 schema creates resources named with the group id (no prefix) and type 'Groups'. If a realm has both V1 and V2 resources (migration scenario), the V1 method would encounter V2 resources (type 'Groups', not 'Group') and skip them (type mismatch), so no crash. But if any resource of type 'Group' lacks the prefix, the substring is unsafe. A length check or startsWith check should be added.

findings.title: canManage() accepts VIEW scope — confirmed high severity privilege escalation
findings.body: This finding reiterates and confirms the critical bug at line 70: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), meaning an admin with only the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type (all groups) passes the manage check. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage() (line 181), which calls canManage(). Therefore, a view-only groups admin can create top-level groups. Similarly, GroupResource.updateGroup (line 120), deleteGroup (line 158), and addChild (line 197) all call requireManage(group) -> canManage(group), which correctly checks only MANAGE (line 79). But the global canManage() (used for creating top-level groups) is broken. The fix: change line 70 to `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`.

findings.title: hasPermission NPE when all-groups resource does not exist — denial of service / 500 error
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 141-150), when groupId is null or the per-group resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 144) and then immediately `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 147) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (line 133-151 of AdminPermissionsSchema: returns null if type is null or resource not found). This happens when: (1) admin permissions are enabled but AdminPermissionsSchema.init was not called (e.g. realm created before feature, or init failed), (2) the 'Groups' resource was deleted manually, (3) the resource server exists but schema resources were not created. The NPE propagates as a 500 error to the admin API caller. Every group permission check (canView, canManage, canViewMembers, etc.) goes through hasPermission, so a missing all-groups resource breaks all group admin endpoints with 500 errors. The fix: add `if (resource == null) return false;` after line 144.

findings.title: hasPermission NPE when all-users resource does not exist — denial of service / 500 error
findings.body: In UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105-114), when the per-user resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 109) and then `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` (line 111) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the 'Users' resource does not exist. This NPE breaks all user permission checks (canView, canManage, canMapRoles, etc.) with a 500 error when the all-users resource is missing. The fix: add `if (resource == null) return false;` after line 109.

findings.title: Cross-realm bypass: canView()/canManage()/canView(group)/canManage(group) lack isAdminSameRealm check
findings.body: This finding consolidates the cross-realm bypass in GroupPermissionsV2: canView() (line 47-53), canView(group) (line 55-62), canManage() (line 64-71), and canManage(group) (line 73-80) all return true based on `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (or MANAGE_USERS) without checking `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. In Keycloak's admin permission model, an admin from a different realm (e.g. master realm admin) with manage-users/view-users roles should not automatically have those rights in the realm being managed. The V1 GroupPermissions.canView(group) (line 254-264) explicitly returns false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V2 overrides omit this check, creating a cross-realm privilege escalation: a master-realm admin with view-users can view all groups in any realm they can access, and with manage-users can create/update/delete groups. The fix: add `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before the role check in all four methods (or at the start of each method).

findings.title: Cross-realm bypass: canView(user)/canManage(user)/canMapRoles/canManageGroupMembership/canImpersonate lack isAdminSameRealm check
findings.body: This finding consolidates the cross-realm bypass in UserPermissionsV2: canView(user) (line 47-53), canManage(user) (line 55-62), canMapRoles(user) (line 77-83), canManageGroupMembership(user) (line 85-92), and canImpersonate(user, requester) (line 65-74) all return true based on `root.hasOneAdminRole(...)` without checking `root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V1 UserPermissions.canView() (line 297-307) and canManage() (line 232-243) explicitly return false when `!root.isAdminSameRealm()`. The V2 overrides omit this check, allowing a master-realm admin with manage-users/view-users/impersonation roles to view, manage, map roles, manage group membership, and impersonate users in any realm they can access. This is a critical cross-realm authorization bypass. The fix: add `if (!root.isAdminSameRealm()) return false;` before the role check in all five methods.
